Overview

A 90-minute paper exam on Weeks 1–5 (all 22 expressions), scored out of 50. It keeps the syllabus format of contextual multiple choice in short real-life stories and adds listening, word order, register, error correction and a short written dialogue.

Change from the syllabus. The syllabus lists a 2–3 minute spoken dialogue for the midterm. This term the midterm is written only. Part 8 (a written dialogue with at least 3 expressions) replaces the speaking task, and the speaking skill is assessed at the Week 11 Final.

Listening audio and script

AudioAbout 1 minute. Play it twice with a 30-second pause.

Two-voice recording made with a speech synthesis engine (American English voices, slightly slower than normal speed). You can also read the script aloud with a colleague.

MikeHey, Rosa! I didn't expect to run into you here.

RosaMike! Hi! My washing machine broke, so I'm killing time while my clothes dry. What about you?

MikeSame thing, actually. I just dropped off my son at practice, and I'm picking up some groceries next door after this.

RosaBusy morning! Hey, how's your new roommate? Do you two get along?

MikeOh, we hit it off right away. We both love cooking. But my old friend Dave stood me up again last night. We planned dinner at seven, and he never came.

RosaAgain? That's the third time, right?

MikeYeah. We used to be really close, but I think we're growing apart.

RosaMaybe you two should talk and patch things up.

MikeMaybe. So, did you figure out the problem with your washing machine?

RosaNot yet. I called the landlord, but he hasn't sorted it out. I almost gave up and bought a new one!

MikeHa! Don't give up. Oh, my dryer's done. I need to head out. Nice running into you!

RosaYou too! See you around.

Answer key

Part 1 · Listening

  1. F They met by chance: “run into you.”
  2. T “We hit it off right away.”
  3. F Dave never came. He stood Mike up.
  4. F “He hasn't sorted it out.”
  5. b waiting and passing the time
  6. a slowly becoming less close
  7. b Mike should talk to Dave and patch things up.
  8. dropped off
  9. get along
  10. head out

Part 2 · Story in Context

  1. c break the ice
  2. d turned around
  3. b came up with
  4. b start over
  5. c shoot the breeze
  6. c gets along with
  7. b drop · off
  8. d sorted out
  9. b came back
  10. a made small talk

Part 3 · What Does It Mean Here?

  1. a I met him by chance.
  2. b buy or get bread
  3. a quit / stopped trying
  4. b They liked each other right away.
  5. c finding a way to manage it

Part 4 · Word Order

  1. b figure it out
  2. b stood her up
  3. a got stood up
  4. b come up with a plan
  5. b into my neighbor

Part 5 · Would You Say This?

  1. b “Shoot the breeze” is casual and a little old-fashioned. It is fine with friends, but too casual for an interview.
  2. a Option b is far too formal for a text to a friend.
  3. a “My bad” and “dude” are slang: recognize them, but don't use them with a manager.
  4. b Both are correct. “Get along” is the everyday U.S. choice; “get on well” is heard more in British English.

Part 6 · Find and Fix

  1. I need to figure it out before Monday.
  2. Can you drop me off at the train station?
  3. He came up with a great idea for the party.
  4. She stood me up last Friday.
  5. My roommate and I get along very well.
  6. We used to be best friends, but we grew apart after high school.

Part 7 · Text Messages

  1. kill time
  2. patched things up
  3. hit it off
  4. pick (you) up
  5. head out

“Grow apart” is the extra expression.

Part 8 · Writing rubric (5 points)

MeaningExpressions are used with the correct meaning.2
FormWord order and tense are correct (figure it out, stood me up).2
Natural and appropriateThe dialogue fits the situation and the register. Three natural expressions score higher than six forced ones.1
